Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, funerals/cemeteries are not impossible triggers, but they are weakly anchored unless there was a death in the accident or major bereavement content. Nothing else in the profile suggests grief- or death-related cueing, so this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for a life-threatening accident. The other items center on fear, disorganization of memory, hypervigilance, and damaged self-view, but do not indicate betrayal by authorities, emergency response, or organizational negligence. This appraisal therefore appears insufficiently supported by the trauma context and accompanying items.

vignette:
Leilani, a 58-year-old psychiatrist of Maori descent, still feels the jolt of the impact when a driver ran a red light and T-boned her sedan two years ago. She had been on her way to an evening shift at the hospital. The wreckage pinned her legs, and she remembers the smell of gasoline and the sound of her own breathing more clearly than any face. In the months since, she has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous-every intersection hides a threat, every driver is one distraction away from catastrophe. That conviction kept pulling her back into the memory of the crash, as though she needed to relive it over and over in order to prove to herself that she had been right all along. This conviction sits at the core of her present suffering, colouring everything.

The sight of a car turning too quickly, or the sudden flash of headlights in her rearview mirror, is enough to drop her straight back into that moment. Each time it happened, she told herself with grim certainty that she would never feel safe again - that the world was a place where catastrophe could strike at any second, and there was nothing she could do to prevent it. She cannot tell a coherent story of what happened, not even to herself-the memories arrive in fragments: the metallic taste, the steering wheel's pressure against her ribs, then a blank until the paramedics. After a memory surfaced, she found her eyes darting to every car on the road, jumping at the sound of a horn, certain that another accident was only seconds away. The sequence is jumbled; she cannot place which came first, the spin or the stop. When these images surge up without warning, they reinforce her sense of permanent damage, as if the accident rewired her entirely. She is no longer the competent psychiatrist she used to be; now she doubts her own judgment, certain she will make the wrong call. Because she was convinced her decisions would lead to harm, she began to withdraw from clinical responsibilities, delegating assessments to colleagues and avoiding any case that required a quick, confident judgment. These appraisals, in turn, make everyday triggers feel sharper-a honk, a brake screech, even the hospital's ambulance bay can send her heart racing.

Leilani has tried to manage by controlling her emotions. She clenches her jaw when unwanted thoughts arrive, refusing to let tears surface. She avoids driving altogether, taking the bus, but even that is difficult: the sudden stop of a bus can trigger the same crash imagery. She has also stopped having sex entirely and, most troublingly, she dreads going to sleep. Lying in the dark, with no visual input, her mind fills with the accident's confused sounds and images. The more she tries to push those memories away, the more they intrude, and the more hypervigilant she becomes. She catches herself sitting with her back to the wall in the staff lounge, scanning the room for exits. And the more intensely she felt that vigilance, the more the details of the crash came rushing in - the shatter of glass, the pressure on her chest - as if the hypervigilance itself had become a gateway to the memory. She wakes several times a night to check that the apartment door is locked, that the smoke detector is quiet, that nothing is wrong. Living at that pitch of alertness, the slightest unexpected noise - a footstep in the hallway, a car engine idling - turned into an unmistakable signal that the world was about to harm her again. Her startle response is extreme: a colleague's sudden tap on her shoulder made her yelp and drop a chart.

Her occupation, once a source of pride, now compounds her distress. She treats trauma survivors, and their stories echo her own fears. She finds herself avoiding certain patients or steering sessions away from car accidents, a maladaptive strategy that only deepens her shame and self-doubt. The memory of the crash surfaces without warning during consultations, blurring her concentration. She cannot tell whether she is overreacting or genuinely unsafe-the world feels too unpredictable to trust.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a moment during a routine supervision meeting. A junior doctor mentioned a near-miss on the highway, and Leilani felt her chest constrict so tightly she excused herself. In the bathroom, she pressed her back against the tiled wall, trembling, convinced she was about to have a heart attack. She realised she could no longer function as a clinician, and that terrified her more than anything. She hopes, she says, to find a way to sleep through the night without checking the locks, and to stop feeling that every car on the road is aimed at her.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that triggers cause negative appraisals (e.g., triggering stimuli leading to distorted beliefs).
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies (e.g., beliefs causing avoidance).
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to memory (e.g., beliefs triggering intrusive recollections).
No paragraph conveys that memory leads to triggers (e.g., memories heightening sensitivity to cues).
No paragraph conveys that threat leads to memory (e.g., feeling unsafe evoking trauma memory).
No paragraph conveys that threat leads to triggers (e.g., threat perception making stimuli more triggering).

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers cause negative appraisals (e.g., triggering stimuli leading to distorted beliefs).
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies (e.g., beliefs causing avoidance).
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to memory (e.g., beliefs triggering intrusive recollections).
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that memory leads to triggers (e.g., memories heightening sensitivity to cues).
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that threat leads to memory (e.g., feeling unsafe evoking trauma memory).
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that threat leads to triggers (e.g., threat perception making stimuli more triggering).
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
